faq.metaDescription: Common questions about the Off Work Countdown timer: overnight shifts, hourly wage calculation, offline use, privacy, and installing it as an app.
faq.heading: Frequently asked questions
faq.intro: Everything about setting up your workday countdown, how the earnings figure is worked out, and what happens to your data.

items.a: It is a free web app that shows exactly how much of your workday is left. You set the time you start and the time you finish, and it counts down the hours, minutes and seconds while a progress bar fills up. There is no account to create and nothing to install.

items.q: How do I set it up?
items.a: Pick your start and end time, then press Start Countdown. Your times are remembered in the browser, so the next time you open the page it is already configured. You can change them at any time by pressing Return.

items.q: Does it work for night shifts that run past midnight?
items.a: Yes. If your end time is earlier than your start time, for example 22:00 to 06:00, the countdown treats it as a shift that crosses midnight. Opening the page at 01:00 correctly shows the shift that began the previous evening rather than starting a new one.

items.q: How is the money earned today calculated?
items.a: Turn on Salary Settings and enter either a monthly or a daily figure. A monthly salary is divided by the number of working days in a month, which defaults to 21.75, to get a daily rate. That daily rate is then multiplied by how much of your shift has elapsed. The How it works page explains where 21.75 comes from and how to change it.

items.q: Will it still remind me if I close the tab?
items.a: The web version can remind you only while its page remains open. The desktop client is built for this job: it keeps the countdown in the system tray when its window is hidden and can send the native reminder from the background.
Yes. The app is a progressive web app, so after your first visit it is cached and keeps working without a connection. The countdown is calculated entirely on your device and never needs the network.

Your working hours and salary stay in your browser's local storage and are never sent to a server. Nobody else can see them, and clearing your browser data removes them. There is an eye button next to the earnings figure that masks the amount when someone is looking over your shoulder. The site does collect anonymous page-view and performance statistics, which contain no personal or salary data.

Yes. Native clients are available for macOS on Apple Silicon and Intel, and for Windows on x64 and ARM64. They add a tray countdown, native reminders, launch at login, a global shortcut and one-click updates. The Download page always points to the latest published installers.

items.q: Is it free, and is the code open?
items.a: It is completely free, with no accounts, adverts or paid tiers. The source code is published on GitHub under the MIT licence, so anyone can read it, host their own copy or contribute changes.

Nineteen, including English, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Hindi, Marathi, Turkish, Arabic, Thai, Indonesian and Vietnamese. The language is picked from your browser settings on the first visit and can be changed from the selector at any time.

howItWorks.metaTitle: How it works - Off Work Countdown
howItWorks.metaDescription: How the workday countdown handles overnight shifts, and how the hourly wage figure is derived from a monthly salary using 21.75 working days.
howItWorks.heading: How it works
howItWorks.intro: A short explanation of the arithmetic behind the countdown, the progress bar and the earnings figure, so you can tell whether the numbers match your own contract.

sections.heading: Defining a shift
body: A shift is simply a start time and an end time. When you press Start Countdown, both are anchored to today's date and the timer runs to the end of that shift.

If the end time is earlier than the start time, the shift is understood to cross midnight. A 22:00 to 06:00 shift opened at 01:00 belongs to the evening that has already begun, not to a new one starting tonight, so the remaining time is five hours rather than twenty-nine.

sections.heading: The progress bar
body: Progress is the share of the shift that has already passed, measured against its full length rather than against a fixed eight hours. A six-hour shift and a twelve-hour shift both read 50 per cent at the halfway point.
The value is clamped between 0 and 100, so arriving early or staying late never pushes the bar outside its range.

sections.heading: Turning a monthly salary into a daily rate
body: If you enter a monthly salary, it has to be converted to a daily rate before it can be spread across the shift. The default divisor is 21.75 working days per month.

That number is not arbitrary. A year has 365 days, of which 104 fall on weekends, leaving 261 working days. Divided across twelve months, that is exactly 21.75. It is the monthly salary base prescribed by regulation in mainland China. If you are employed somewhere else, or your contract counts differently, treat it as a starting point rather than a rule — your own contract is what decides.

If your contract counts differently, for example a six-day week or a four-day week, change the working days per month field and every figure updates accordingly. Entering a daily salary directly skips this step altogether.

sections.heading: Earnings during the shift
body: The amount shown is the daily rate multiplied by the proportion of the shift completed, updated once a second. At the halfway point you have earned half the daily rate; when the countdown reaches zero the full amount is shown.
This is a straight-line estimate. It does not model overtime multipliers, unpaid breaks, bonuses, tax or social insurance, so treat it as a rough sense of progress rather than a payslip.

sections.heading: Where your data lives
body: Your hours, salary and preferences are written to your browser's local storage on the device you are using. They are never transmitted to a server, so they are not synchronised between your phone and your computer, and clearing your browser data erases them.
Because everything is computed locally, the app also works with no connection at all once it has been loaded once.

about.metaDescription: About Off Work Countdown, a free and open-source local-first workday timer for the web, macOS and Windows.
about.heading: About Off Work Countdown
about.intro: A small, open-source tool built to make the remaining workday understandable at a glance — without accounts, adverts or sending your schedule and salary to a server.

sections.heading: Why this project exists
body: A workday is easier to reason about when the remaining time, completed percentage and optional earnings estimate are visible in one calm interface. Off Work Countdown turns those numbers into a lightweight utility that can stay open all day.
The web app works offline after the first visit. The desktop client adds a tray countdown, a compact companion window, native reminders, launch at login and a global shortcut.

sections.heading: Local-first and private
body: Your working hours, workdays, salary and preferences stay on your device. The countdown and earnings estimate are computed locally. The desktop client contains no analytics and does not send these settings or a user identifier to our servers.

The web version uses privacy-conscious page-view and performance measurement plus a small set of aggregate product events. Those product events contain only an event name — never your schedule, salary, account or advertising identifier. As with any website, hosting and analytics providers may receive ordinary connection metadata such as an IP address and user agent under their own terms.

sections.heading: What the desktop client connects to
body: The desktop client works locally and does not require an account. On launch it asks GitHub whether a newer version exists; that request carries no account, salary, or usage data, and the installer itself is downloaded only after you choose to update. It also reaches the network when you open an external link or pick a social sharing service. Those third-party destinations apply their own terms and privacy policies.

Native reminders are scheduled and displayed by your operating system. Countdown settings are kept in the application's local data store and can be removed by uninstalling the app and deleting its application data.

sections.heading: Important limits
body: Salary and time totals are estimates for personal reference. They are not payroll records and are not legal, tax, employment or financial advice. Reminders and update checks are convenience features and should not be relied on for safety-critical or legally required timing.
The software is provided under the MIT licence, as is and without warranty, to the extent permitted by law. The licence text in the repository is the controlling legal notice.

sections.heading: Free and open source
body: The project is released under the MIT licence. You can inspect the code, report a bug, suggest an improvement or build your own version from the public GitHub repository.

privacy.metaDescription: What Off Work Countdown stores on your device, the little it measures, and who else is involved. No accounts, no advertising, no salary data leaving your device.
privacy.heading: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: Off Work Countdown is built so the numbers you care about — your hours and what you have earned — never leave your device. This page sets out exactly what that means, and what the small amount of remaining data is for.

sections.heading: What stays on your device
body: Everything you enter is stored locally: in your browser's local storage on the web, and in the application's own data folder in the desktop client. It is not uploaded, and there is no account system to attach it to even if we wanted one.
The countdown, the progress bar and the earnings estimate are all calculated on your device from these values.
bullets: Start and end times, workdays, lunch break and overtime
Notification, health reminder and mini timer preferences
Theme, language and the woodfish tap count

sections.heading: What the website measures
body: The site measures two things. The first is page views and loading performance, through Vercel's cookieless analytics. The second is a small set of aggregate product counters that tell us which features get used at all.

A product event is one word from a fixed, public list — for example share_open or countdown_start — recorded as a per-day tally. Nothing is attached to it: no identifier, no session, no schedule, no salary. A number that counts how many people opened the share panel today cannot be traced back to any of them.

The full list of events lives in the open-source repository, so this is something you can verify rather than take on trust. As with any website, our hosting and analytics providers receive ordinary connection metadata such as an IP address and browser identification in order to serve the page; we do not store it or build profiles from it.

sections.heading: Cookies
body: The site sets one cookie: i18nextLng. It holds a language code so the next page you open is already in the language you picked, and it is written only after you choose a language. It lasts a year and you can delete it at any time along with the rest of the site data.
There are no advertising or cross-site tracking cookies. The measurement described above is cookieless.

sections.heading: Sharing a countdown
body: A share link carries only the start and end time, encoded in the URL. Salary is never included — not hidden, not encoded, simply not there. Whoever opens your link sees a schedule and nothing about your pay.
When you pick a social service to share through, you leave this site and that service's own privacy policy takes over.

sections.heading: The desktop client
body: The desktop client contains no usage analytics. The measurement code is not merely switched off — it is removed at build time, so it is not present in the application you install.

The version downloaded from GitHub checks on launch whether a newer release exists. That request carries no account, salary or usage data, and the installer is downloaded only after you decide to update. If GitHub cannot be reached directly, you can retry through a third-party mirror; either way the downloaded update is signature-checked before it is installed.
The version installed from the Microsoft Store makes no update requests at all. Updates are delivered by the Store, and the in-app update entry simply opens the Store listing.
Reminders are scheduled and displayed by your operating system on your machine. The client also reaches the network when you open an external link or choose a social service to share through.

sections.heading: Who else is involved
body: Running a website means other companies handle parts of it. These are all of them:
bullets: Vercel — hosting, page-view and performance measurement
Upstash — stores the aggregate product counters
GitHub — release information and installer downloads
Microsoft — distribution and updates for the Microsoft Store version
A third-party download mirror, only when you choose to retry through it
The social service you pick when you share a countdown

sections.heading: Removing your data
body: On the web, clearing this site's data in your browser removes everything, including the language cookie. In the desktop client, uninstalling the application and then deleting its data folder does the same.
Because none of it reaches us in the first place, there is nothing to request from us and nothing for us to delete on your behalf.

sections.heading: Changes to this page
body: If this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it, and anything material is called out in the release notes. Past versions are visible in the repository's history.

sections.heading: Getting in touch
body: Questions about anything here are welcome as an issue on GitHub. If something in this policy does not match what the code does, that is a bug worth reporting — the code is public and can be checked against every claim on this page.
